source.title: Quality Not Quantity: On the Interaction between Dataset Design and Robustness of CLIP
source.authors: Thao Nguyen; Gabriel Ilharco; Mitchell Wortsman; Sewoong Oh; Ludwig Schmidt

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present and readable, including appendices; some equations and symbols show minor extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training-set size and measures downstream zero-shot classification error, a different measure and setting from the language-model scaling claims. This bears on V6 only; it does not test language-model pretraining loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses empirical scaling laws and cites prior work, but does not test the claimed language-model laws. Its own Appendix C reports CLIP zero-shot classification error across training-data sizes; it says data efficiency varies significantly by evaluation setting. It does not fit power laws or test extrapolation. Other scaling-law results cited from prior work are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study is about how pre-training data sources affect CLIP's effective robustness. It does not test any version of the scaling claim. Its only scaling result is a preliminary figure (Appendix C, Fig. 17) of zero-shot error against 1M–15M samples. The authors say it used minimal hyperparameter tuning, and they fit no power law and test no extrapolation. They conclude only that data efficiency differs by source and test set, which says nothing about whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. The accuracy-on-the-line linear trends relate in-distribution to out-of-distribution accuracy, a different construct from scaling. Scaling laws appear only as related work and future directions.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors' main conclusions are threefold. Robustness induced by the six CLIP pre-training sources varies across distribution shifts, with no source dominating. Mixing sources, by input mixing or ensembling, dilutes the robustness of the best source, interpolating between their trends. Filtering a noisy source with a robust model can improve robustness, so quality matters more than quantity. The data-scaling experiments are a minor, preliminary appendix result offered as a future direction, not a main conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CLIP zero-shot classification error over pre-training sample-count sweeps, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Data efficiency varies with evaluation setting; the paper also studies multiple pre-training data sources.

fits_no_version.finding: CLIP (ResNet-50) zero-shot error falls with pre-training samples from 1M to 15M. The rate of decrease differs significantly across six data sources and five test sets (Appendix C, Fig. 17), with no fitted functional form.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The data-scaling rate of downstream zero-shot error in image-text models depends on the pre-training data source and the evaluation distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Probit-transformed accuracy on a shifted test set is linear in ImageNet accuracy, with a slope set by the training distribution. The authors describe this effective robustness as independent of training-set size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effective robustness (the slope of the accuracy-on-the-line relation) is invariant to training-set size and set by the data distribution.

record.problems: The pre-training datasets are limited to 5M–15M samples, and the paper says the data-scaling experiments use minimal hyperparameter tuning. It reports no power-law fits or extrapolation tests for these curves; Figure 17 plots values averaged over 3 random seeds without stated error bars.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss is measured.
All: only ResNet-50 is used, and shape is not varied.
Power-law form in image-text models: the CLIP data-scaling curves are plotted, but no power-law fit is made or assessed.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss: error falls with more data, but neither predictability nor a functional form is tested.
All: no exponents are fitted, so fit-dependence cannot be assessed.

record.verdict_notes: This is not a scaling-laws study. The reader over-linked the single appendix figure to V6. Effective robustness is invariant to data size, per the cited Miller et al. work. Scaling laws are discussed only in Section 7.2.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from power laws fit on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, including its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture details on held-out language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures downstream performance as training-set size varies, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a predictive scaling law.
Dependence of fitted exponents, compute-optimal allocation, and curve bending on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: CLIP (aggregate across six pre-training sources)
rows.size_stated: ResNet-50 image encoder; training subsets range from 1M to a maximum of 15M samples
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of pre-training samples and measured zero-shot classification error; plotted errors averaged over 3 random seeds.

conditions.value: YFCC, LAION, RedCaps, WIT, CC-12M, Shutterstock (aggregate)

rows.measure: Data efficiency: change in zero-shot classification error with increasing pre-training sample count
rows.value: Data efficiency varies significantly depending on the evaluation setting.
rows.uncertainty: not stated; plotted error values are averaged over 3 random seeds
rows.locator: Appendix C, Figure 17 and accompanying description
rows.note: Aggregate result stated by the authors; Figure 17 shows the separate source-by-evaluation curves, but the text does not give their individual numerical values.
rows.check: The row records that data efficiency varies by evaluation setting. That is a comparison of error-reduction rates across sources and test sets, not a test of whether downstream performance scales predictably (V6) or follows a power law in another modality (V5). There is no fit, no extrapolation, and no numbers are given. The finding belongs under fits_no_version, not as V6 evidence. The 'partial' state has no baseline for the version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.reason: The study reports that data efficiency differs significantly by evaluation setting, so downstream performance scaling is not uniform across the tested settings; this does not establish a power-law fit or predictive extrapolation (r1).
